Question: What can you tell about a publisher's expectations for sales of a book, based on the amount of the advance?
Answer: The publisher will have run a costing which estimates how many books they’re going to sell in the foreseeable future (which is usually a year or two from publication) and how much the royalty income would be from that level of sales. That’s really the basis for what’s an affordable advance level. Of course, if you really really want the book and get into an auction, you’re likely to be pushed higher than that. The proportion of the advance that is above the level you worked out in the costing is called the ‘unearned’, and publishers try to minimise this, but it’s not actually unusual to be carrying an unearned advance on a book. (This is distinct from a book ‘not earning out’ its advance.) In order to work out the sales expectation based on the advance level you will need to estimate certain things that aren’t public knowledge such as the royalty rates payable on the various formats, the retailer discounts, returns rates and so on.

Question: Can one write a sequel to one of Stephen King's novels and send it to him for approval, or does one need approval before writing it? If so, how should one go about contacting Stephen King to get approval to write a sequel?
Answer: You can if you wish write a sequel. You cannot publish or distribute it without his permission, because it would be a derivative work of his original novel and thus still his intellectual property. Let’s be real here: although Stephen King seems like a mensch, the chances of him even reading it, let alone giving you permission to publish it, are absolute zero. You could write to him care of his literary agent. I honestly wouldn’t bother though. If you just want people to read it, I would suggest that a fanfic platform like AO3 is the way to go. Just be aware that if King ever caught wind of it and wanted it to be removed, AO3 would have to comply.

Question: Is anyone else disturbed by the way droids are treated in Star Wars, since they’re as intelligent and emotional as humans?
Answer: The dirty little secret of Star Wars is that it is in many ways an antebellum slavers’ paradise. Droids are obviously sentient, thinking, feeling beings who are enslaved. Obviously! And terrible things happen to them, by the standards we generally set of people. For example, droids develop distinct quirks and personalities over time, based on their experiences. This is inconvenient to the slave masters, who have their slaves’ memories wiped periodically to prevent it. The wrinkle Star Wars adds is a Tom Show one: for the most part the droids are happy slaves who Know Their Place. While there are, in canon, a couple of forays into this whole issue - L3–37’s droid rebellion in Solo, the droid bar in The Mandalorian - it all gets dropped pretty quickly. We don’t want to be thinking ‘so I guess Luke is one of those good slave masters who really loves his slaves’ and so on. (The reason this stuff exists to begin with is because George Lucas was homaging The Hidden Fortress, in which the POV characters are two Japanese feudal serfs who are caught up in a clash of nobles.)
